question: Which body weight did Hughes et al. use inside Cockcroft-Gault to compute the CrCl covariate?

source_facts.fact: Creatinine clearance was calculated with the Cockcroft-Gault formula (reference 41). No weight basis or cap is stated.
CrCl mean 80.1, SD 29.5, median 75.5, range 36-211 mL/min; total body weight mean 88.8 kg, range 48-152 kg; FFM mean 57.7, median 58.4 kg.

CrCl enters as a precomputed data column named CRCL2; the stream normalizes with RF=CRCL2/90 and comments '90' as the mean CrCl. The FFM normalizer 55 is likewise commented as the mean, although Table 1 reports a mean of 57.7 kg.

reconstruction.method: Virtual population matched to Table 1 marginals (sex mix, age, total weight, height range, serum creatinine) under assumed joint structure; Cockcroft-Gault applied with each candidate weight. Simulated FFM (mean 57.5 kg) reproduces Table 1 FFM (57.7 kg), which checks the body-size assumptions independently of CrCl.
reconstruction.robustness: Closest basis was ideal body weight in all three tested scenarios (height-weight correlation 0.5 or 0.7; pooled or sex-specific serum creatinine).

ideal_body_weight_devine.summary: Reproduces the Table 1 CrCl mean and median within about 2 mL/min.

adjusted_body_weight_0_4.summary: About 12 mL/min above Table 1, but its simulated mean (about 93) is close to the control stream's 'mean CrCl 90' comment.

total_body_weight.summary: About 29 mL/min above the Table 1 mean; inconsistent with both Table 1 and the control-stream comment.

decision.resolution_path: Ask the corresponding author what weight produced the CRCL2 column and whether any cap applied. A documented answer replaces this assessment with a new version.

limits: Indirect evidence from marginal summary statistics with an assumed joint distribution.
Does not establish the authors' method, assay, rounding or capping.
Applies to the Hughes 2019 covariate definition only. Other models define their own renal covariates.
